title: Best Vodka for No Hangover: What Matters More Than the Brand
excerpt: Is there a vodka that won't give you a hangover? Why vodka is one of the cleanest drinks, whether expensive vodka helps, flavored vs plain, the best mixers, and why how much you drink matters most.
metaDescription: Is there a vodka that won't give you a hangover? Why vodka is a cleaner choice, whether premium vodka helps, the best mixers, and why amount matters most.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no vodka that gives you no hangover. Ethanol, the alcohol itself, causes most of what you feel the next morning, and every vodka is mostly ethanol and water. What vodka does have going for it is that it's one of the cleanest drinks you can choose. It contains very few congeners, the extra compounds that give darker drinks their flavor and that research links to worse hangovers. So the "best" vodka for a gentler morning is less about the brand and more about three things: an **unflavored** bottle from a reputable producer, a **clean mixer**, and **how much you drink**. A $60 bottle won't save you from eight drinks, and a decent $15 bottle is fine for four.

**The quick rules:** pick a plain, unflavored vodka from a well-known producer (price matters much less than you think). Skip sugary flavored vodkas and premixed cocktails. Mix with soda water, fresh citrus, or plain juice rather than energy drinks or sugary sodas. Eat before you start, pace yourself to about one drink an hour, and drink a glass of water between rounds. Stop a drink or two earlier than you think you need to.

> **A quick note on safety.** This guide is about choosing vodka and drinking it sensibly. It isn't medical advice. Vodka is easy to drink fast because it has so little flavor, and that makes it easy to overdo. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has cold, pale, or bluish skin, or has a seizure. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover, so don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." Never drink anything sold as alcohol that didn't come from a licensed store or bar; homemade or counterfeit spirits can contain dangerous amounts of methanol. And if you regularly feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you go without a drink, talk to a doctor, because that can be a sign your body has come to depend on alcohol.

## Why Vodka Is One of the Least-Hangover Drinks

To understand why vodka has a reputation as a "clean" drink, it helps to know what actually causes a hangover.

**Ethanol does most of the damage.** Alcohol disrupts your sleep, especially the deeper, more restful stages in the second half of the night. It makes you lose more fluid than you take in. It irritates your stomach lining. It triggers an inflammatory response in the body. And while your liver breaks it down, it produces a short-lived but toxic compound called **acetaldehyde**. All of that happens no matter what you drink. Our guide on [why vodka hangovers happen](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) goes through each of these in more detail.

**Congeners add to it.** Congeners are the small amounts of other chemicals produced during fermentation and aging, things like methanol, fusel alcohols, aldehydes, and compounds pulled out of wooden barrels. They're what give whiskey, brandy, dark rum, and red wine their color and depth of flavor. They're also suspected of making hangovers worse. You can read more in our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

Vodka is made specifically to strip those compounds out. It's distilled to a very high strength, usually in column stills, then diluted and often filtered. The goal is a spirit that is clean and neutral. That's why vodka sits at the low end of every congener ranking, alongside gin and white rum, and well below bourbon, brandy, and whiskey.

### What the research actually shows

Two studies get cited most often, and both are real:

- **Vodka vs. bourbon (2010).** Researchers led by Damaris Rohsenow at Brown University gave healthy young adults enough bourbon or vodka to reach a fairly high blood alcohol level, then measured how they felt the next morning. The study, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*, found that bourbon produced somewhat worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level. It also found that both drinks impaired next-day attention and reaction time about equally. In other words, choosing vodka may make you feel a little better, but it doesn't make you any sharper.
- **Vodka vs. brandy (1970s).** An earlier British study by G.L.S. Pawan compared vodka with brandy, a spirit high in congeners, and reported more hangover symptoms after brandy.

The takeaway is consistent: **at the same amount of alcohol, a low-congener drink like vodka tends to produce a milder hangover than a dark spirit. But the difference is modest, and the amount you drink matters far more.** If vodka leads you to drink more because it goes down easily, you can easily lose the benefit.

For a ranking of common drinks from least to most hangover-prone, see our guide to the [least hangover-prone alcohol](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked).

## Does Expensive Vodka Give You Less of a Hangover?

This is the question most people are really asking. The honest answer: **mostly no, with a couple of caveats.**

Here's why price matters less with vodka than with almost any other drink.

**The rules leave little room for "dirty" vodka.** In the US, vodka has to be distilled from a fermented base and bottled at no less than 40% alcohol by volume. In the EU, it must be at least 37.5% and is subject to legal limits on methanol. A cheap, legally sold vodka from a large distillery and a premium one are both, chemically, very close to pure ethanol and water. The flavor differences people taste are real but small, and they come from tiny amounts of compounds well below anything likely to affect how you feel the next day.

**Big producers are very good at this.** Modern column stills from large, established distilleries produce a very consistent, very clean spirit. Some of the "bottom shelf" vodkas in the US are made by the same large companies that make mid-shelf brands. Being cheap doesn't mean being poorly made.

**Where cheap can be worse, in practice:**

- **Harsh vodka gets mixed with sugar.** If a vodka tastes rough, people tend to mix it with sugary sodas, energy drinks, or sweet premixes to cover it up. That sugar and caffeine can make the morning worse in its own right.
- **Bigger bottles, bigger pours.** A plastic 1.75-liter "handle" at a party tends to get poured freely. That's a dosage problem, not a vodka problem, but it's real.
- **Unregulated alcohol is a different story.** Counterfeit or homemade spirits, which are a known problem in some countries and tourist areas, can contain dangerous methanol. That's not a hangover issue. It can cause blindness or death. Buy from licensed stores and bars.

**Where expensive doesn't help:**

- **"Distilled six times" or "filtered through diamonds" is marketing.** Extra distillation and fancy filtration can change the texture and taste slightly, but there's no good evidence that they make any difference to hangovers once a vodka is already clean.
- **A smoother vodka can make you drink more.** If a premium bottle goes down easily, you may simply drink more of it. That more than wipes out any small difference.

For vodka, the practical answer is simple: spend what you like for taste, but don't pay extra expecting a better morning.

## Does Filtering Cheap Vodka Make It Better?

You may have heard that running cheap vodka through a water-filter pitcher several times turns it into "premium" vodka. Charcoal filtering is part of how many vodkas are made, so the idea isn't crazy, and some people do report that it tastes a bit smoother afterward.

But a household water filter isn't designed for high-strength spirits, and it won't meaningfully reduce the alcohol, which is what causes the hangover. Any change in taste is small. If you want a smoother drink, the simplest option is to buy a vodka you like the taste of. If you want a gentler morning, drink less of whatever you have.

## Grain, Potato, Corn, or Grape: Does the Base Matter?

Vodka can be made from almost anything that ferments: wheat, rye, corn, potatoes, grapes, even milk whey. The base affects the flavor and feel, especially in vodkas that are distilled less aggressively to keep some character. It has much less effect on hangovers.

- **Wheat vodkas** tend to be soft and slightly sweet. Grey Goose and Absolut are well-known examples.
- **Rye vodkas** often have a bit of spice. Belvedere, from Poland, is a well-known rye vodka.
- **Corn vodkas** are often described as slightly sweet and round. Tito's Handmade Vodka is made from corn.
- **Potato vodkas** usually have a creamier, heavier texture. Chopin is a well-known potato vodka from Poland.
- **Grape vodkas** like Cîroc are made from grapes rather than grain.

One technical note: potatoes and fruit contain pectin, which can produce a bit more methanol during fermentation than grain does. Legally sold vodkas are kept within strict limits, and the amounts involved are tiny, so there's no good evidence that a well-made potato or grape vodka gives a worse hangover than a grain one. What you choose comes down to taste.

### Gluten-free vodka

Distillation removes gluten proteins, so distilled vodka made from wheat or rye is generally considered gluten-free, and major celiac organizations have said so. Some people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity still prefer vodkas made from corn, potatoes, or grapes for peace of mind. That's a reasonable personal choice, but it's about gluten, not hangovers. There's no good evidence that a corn or potato vodka causes a milder hangover in people without a gluten problem.

## Popular Vodkas: An Honest Look

There isn't a ranking of vodkas by hangover, because no good study has compared brands. What follows is a fair, general look at well-known bottles and what you can and can't expect from each. All of them are unflavored, legally regulated vodkas, so the morning after will depend mainly on how much you drink.

| Vodka | Base | What people like | What to keep in mind |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tito's Handmade** | Corn | Widely available, mid-price, smooth, gluten-free made from corn | No evidence it causes fewer hangovers than other clean vodkas |
| **Smirnoff No. 21** | Grain | Very affordable and consistent | Easy to pour heavily from big bottles; flavored Smirnoff products are a different story |
| **Absolut** | Wheat | Clean, classic, widely available | Plain Absolut is fine; the flavored versions add flavorings and are often mixed sweet |
| **Ketel One** | Wheat | Crisp, popular for martinis | Price reflects taste, not a better morning |
| **Grey Goose** | Wheat | Soft, premium feel | You're paying for brand and texture; no hangover advantage has been shown |
| **Belvedere** | Rye | Character and a little spice | A premium price that won't change your hangover |
| **Chopin** | Potato | Creamy texture, good for sipping cold | Potato base is a taste choice, not a health choice |
| **Store brands (e.g., Kirkland)** | Varies | Low price, often good quality | Watch your pours with big bottles |

**Honest bottom line on brands:** any of these, drunk in moderation with a clean mixer, is about as hangover-friendly as alcohol gets. None of them will prevent a hangover if you drink a lot. If you're choosing between a cheap bottle you'll mix with energy drink and a mid-price bottle you'll drink with soda and lime, the mixer choice probably matters more than the bottle.

## Flavored Vodka and Hangovers

Flavored vodkas are where the "vodka is clean" idea starts to break down.

**Added sugar.** Many flavored vodkas, especially the dessert-style ones like whipped cream, cake, or candy flavors, have sugar and flavorings added after distillation. They can also be bottled at lower strength, around 30 to 35% alcohol, which makes them go down even more easily.

**Labels don't always tell you.** In the US, spirits labels generally don't list ingredients or sugar content the way food labels do, so you often can't tell how much sugar is in a flavored bottle just by reading it.

**Why it matters for the morning.** There's no strong evidence that sugar itself causes hangovers. But sweet drinks are easy to drink fast and in large amounts, which raises your blood alcohol, and that's what drives a bad morning. Sweet drinks also make it harder to keep track of how much you've had.

If you like a flavored drink, a better option is plain vodka with something real added: a squeeze of fresh lemon or lime, a few muddled berries, cucumber, or a splash of juice. You get the flavor and you know exactly what's in the glass.

## The Mixer Matters as Much as the Vodka

Because vodka adds so little on its own, what you mix it with makes up a big part of what you're drinking. Some good and bad choices:

**Better choices:**

- **Soda water with fresh lime or lemon.** No sugar, no caffeine, and the bubbles make a drink last longer. A vodka soda is one of the simplest low-hangover drinks there is.
- **Plain juice in modest amounts.** Orange juice (a screwdriver), grapefruit juice, or cranberry juice add some sugar but no caffeine. Using less juice and more soda water helps.
- **Tomato juice (a Bloody Mary).** Gives you some food-like substance and salt, though watch for very salty or spicy premixes.

**Worse choices:**

- **Energy drinks.** Caffeine can mask how drunk you feel, which can lead you to drink more than you realize. It can also make it harder to sleep, and poor sleep is one of the biggest drivers of a hangover.
- **Sugary sodas and premixed cocktail mixers.** Easy to drink quickly, and usually high in sugar.
- **Diet sodas, as a special case.** Some research has found that mixing alcohol with diet soda leads to a higher breath alcohol level than mixing with regular soda, likely because sugar slows how quickly alcohol leaves the stomach. That's not a reason to switch to sugary soda, but it is a reason to go slower with diet mixers.

Carbonation in general may speed up how fast alcohol gets absorbed. The practical response isn't to avoid soda water. It's to sip, not gulp.

## Why How Much You Drink Matters More Than the Brand

If you only take away one point, make it this one. The single biggest factor in your hangover is how much alcohol you drink and how fast you drink it. Brand, price, and base come a distant second.

**What counts as one drink.** In the US, a standard drink of vodka is about 1.5 ounces (a "shot") of 80-proof vodka, which contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. Many bar pours and home-poured drinks are bigger than that. A tall vodka soda poured by eye can easily hold two or three standard drinks.

**Why vodka is easy to overdo.** It's nearly flavorless, it mixes into anything, and it's often drunk as shots. All of that makes it easy to drink a lot quickly without noticing. Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, though this varies a lot from person to person. Drinking faster than that makes your blood alcohol climb.

**Practical ways to keep the dose sensible:**

- **Measure your pours at home.** Use a jigger or a shot glass instead of free-pouring.
- **Use more mixer.** A longer drink takes longer to finish.
- **Pace yourself.** Aim for about one drink an hour, and slow down if shots are being passed around.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows you down and helps with fluid loss.
- **Eat first.** Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed, which keeps your peak lower.
- **Decide your limit before you start.** It's much easier to stick to a number you chose while sober.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers these habits and the evidence behind them.

## Vodka vs. Other Clear Spirits

If you're choosing a low-congener drink, vodka has company.

- **Gin** is essentially vodka flavored with juniper and other botanicals. It's also low in congeners. Most gin hangovers come from the tonic, the amount, and the pace, not the gin itself. See our guide to [gin hangovers](/never-hungover/gin-hangover).
- **White (unaged) rum** is lower in congeners than dark rum, though it varies more between producers.
- **Blanco tequila** made from 100% agave is a reasonable choice, but cheap "mixto" tequilas are a different matter. Our [tequila hangover guide](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth) explains the difference.

Among the clear spirits, plain vodka is the most consistent. If what you want is the cleanest base with the fewest variables, an unflavored vodka is about as good as it gets.

## What to Do If You Wake Up With a Vodka Hangover

Even with a clean drink, too much is too much. If you wake up feeling rough:

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Sip water through the morning. An electrolyte drink can help if you were sweating or vomiting.
- **Eat something gentle.** Toast, crackers, eggs, or a banana. Food can help settle your stomach and steady your blood sugar.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** If you take one, ibuprofen with food is the usual choice for a headache. Avoid acetaminophen (Tylenol) after heavy drinking unless a doctor has said it's fine, because it adds work for your liver.
- **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Another drink just postpones the hangover.
- **Rest.** Time is the only thing that fully fixes a hangover.

**When to see a doctor rather than ride it out:** if you can't keep fluids down for many hours, are vomiting blood, have severe stomach pain, feel confused, or have a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, get medical help. Feeling shaky, sweaty, or anxious every time you stop drinking is also worth raising with a doctor, without judgment, because it can mean your body has started to depend on alcohol.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people add a supplement to their routine on nights out. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe or change how alcohol affects your judgment or driving.

If you want to try it alongside the habits above, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Think of it as a possible extra, not a substitute for drinking less, eating, and hydrating.
Price is the other question people ask. Our look at [cheap vs expensive alcohol and hangovers](/never-hungover/cheap-vs-expensive-alcohol-hangover) explains when paying more for a bottle actually changes how you feel the next day, and when it's mostly marketing.

## The Bottom Line

- **No vodka prevents a hangover.** Ethanol causes most of the symptoms, and all vodka is mostly ethanol.
- **Vodka is one of the cleaner choices.** It's very low in congeners, and research suggests low-congener drinks cause somewhat milder hangovers than dark spirits at the same dose.
- **Price matters much less than you think.** Legally sold vodkas are all close to pure ethanol and water. Pay for taste, not for a better morning.
- **Choose plain over flavored**, and pick a clean mixer like soda water and citrus rather than energy drinks or sugary premixes.
- **How much and how fast you drink matters most.** Measure pours, pace yourself, eat, and alternate with water.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best vodka for no hangover?**

No vodka can guarantee no hangover, because the alcohol itself causes most hangover symptoms. The best choice is a plain, unflavored vodka from a reputable, licensed producer, mixed with soda water or a light mixer and drunk in moderation. Popular options include Tito's, Absolut, Ketel One, and Smirnoff, but there's no good evidence that any one brand causes fewer hangovers than another clean vodka. How much you drink matters far more than which bottle you choose.

**Does expensive vodka give you less of a hangover?**

Not in any meaningful way. Legally sold vodkas are distilled to a very high purity and are mostly ethanol and water, so a cheap bottle from a large, established distillery and a premium one are chemically very similar. Premium vodkas may taste smoother, but there's no good evidence that they cause milder hangovers. Cheap vodka tends to cause trouble indirectly, when people mix it with sugary drinks or pour it freely from large bottles.

**Is vodka better than whiskey for hangovers?**

Probably somewhat. A 2010 study comparing bourbon and vodka at the same blood alcohol level found that bourbon caused slightly worse hangovers, likely because dark spirits contain more congeners. The same study found both drinks impaired next-day attention and reaction time about equally. So vodka may help you feel a little better, but it won't keep you sharp if you drink a lot.

**Does potato vodka or grain vodka cause a worse hangover?**

There's no good evidence that either base causes a worse hangover. Potatoes can produce a bit more methanol during fermentation than grains, but legally sold vodkas are kept within strict limits and the amounts are tiny. The base mainly affects taste and texture: potato vodkas tend to feel creamier, wheat softer, rye spicier, and corn slightly sweeter.

**Does flavored vodka give you a worse hangover?**

It can, mostly indirectly. Many flavored vodkas, especially dessert flavors, have added sugar and flavorings, and they go down easily, which makes it easy to drink more and faster. That higher dose of alcohol is the main problem. If you want flavor, plain vodka with fresh citrus, berries, or a splash of juice gives you more control over what's in your glass.

**What should I mix vodka with to avoid a hangover?**

Soda water with fresh lime or lemon is one of the best options: no sugar, no caffeine, and it makes the drink last longer. Plain juices in modest amounts are fine. Avoid energy drinks, because caffeine can mask how drunk you feel and disrupt your sleep, and go easy on sugary sodas and premixed mixers. Some research suggests diet mixers can raise breath alcohol more than sugary ones, so sip those slowly.

**Does filtering cheap vodka through a water filter reduce hangovers?**

No. Running vodka through a household water filter may slightly change its taste, but it doesn't meaningfully reduce the alcohol, which is what causes the hangover. If you want a smoother drink, buy a vodka you enjoy. If you want a better morning, drink less and pace yourself.

**How many vodka drinks can I have without a hangover?**

There's no safe number that works for everyone, because hangovers depend on your body size, sex, genetics, food, sleep, and how fast you drink. Many people find that sticking to one or two standard drinks (about 1.5 ounces of 80-proof vodka each), spaced out with food and water, rarely causes much of a hangover. The more you drink beyond that, and the faster you drink it, the more likely you are to feel it the next day.
